\textbf{Remark.}\;%
Observation~1 assumes degeneration and source attribution. Under \emph{semantic} evaluation, the equivalence additionally requires \emph{answer alignment}: $P(c_i \text{ supports } a_i) \geq P(c_i \text{ supports } a')$ for $a' \neq a_i$, which is structurally motivated and empirically validated ($\mathrm{BR} \in [1.66,\, 4.97]$; Appendix Table~\ref{tab:frontier-scb}), but could fail if $f$ systematically extracted premises contradicting their source trace's conclusion.
Since Observation~1 shows SICA reduces to majority vote under degeneration, $\mathrm{BR} \geq 1$ follows from the trace-count geometry; the empirical BR consistently exceeds this floor ($1.66\times$--$4.97\times$; Appendix Table~\ref{tab:frontier-scb}), reflecting both base-rate effects and extraction alignment.

tool_args.old_text:
\looseness=-1
Our central finding is that formal verification's value depends on the \emph{independence} of its inputs, not the soundness of its logic. SICA reduces to majority vote under source-attribution scoring (Observation~1), and 27 training-free variants fail to escape---symbolic confirmation bias holds across nine models (7B to frontier), scaling redundancy rather than information. Three zero-cost diagnostics predict failure modes from a $K{=}12$ pilot run (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic-framework}). Cross-architecture verification provides a preliminary escape: gains follow an exploratory capability-gap pattern ($n{=}6$)---positive only when the verifier exceeds the generator's accuracy (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}), suggesting that future self-verification should prioritize \emph{architectural diversity} over scale.

\looseness=-1
More broadly, our DPI bound $I(C;Y) \leq I(T;Y)$ explains why trained verifiers---process reward models \citep{lightman2024prm} and Math-Shepherd \citep{wang2024mathshepherd}---circumvent the self-extraction ceiling: they introduce external training signal that breaks the $M{\to}T{\to}A{\to}C$ Markov chain, providing information about $Y$ not mediated by the model's own traces. For test-time compute scaling, this implies that adding traces from the same model yields diminishing returns once $K_\text{eff}$ saturates; gains require either architectural diversity or external supervision.
